name: Malimba
autonymMeaning: the children of the ancestor Elimbe
place: Urban chiefdom, between Dizangué and Logasse (Sanaga-Maritime, Littoral)
overview: A small Sawa fishing people, the Malimba say they descend from Elimbe, son of Bendi, the ancestor who came from Congo. Settled along the Sanaga and the ocean, between Dizangué and Logasse, alongside the Duala, Bakoko, Banen and Babimbi, they honour the water spirits through the jengu and celebrate the ihangabinde every year.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Minority group, alongside the more numerous Babimbi, and the Duala, Bakoko and Banen; the Malimba also speak Basaa and Bakoko.
Malimba is also spoken in Mouanko and Manoka (Douala).
Homogeneous group: marriages take place mainly within the group and with neighbours.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Ancestral land, to which one is bound as by the umbilical cord: every Malimba must feel at home there.
Having come from the Congo behind the founder Bendi, they lived on the Dibamba, at Dizangué, at Mouanko and on the ocean shore; all know themselves to be descendants of the same ancestor.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Four groups each had their own chief under the Germans; under the French administration, they united under a single chief.
Decisions are made at the chiefdom, or at the canton between villages, by consensus among notables, heads of family, and village and canton chiefs.
The widow is free; formerly, unmarried people only courted after their parents' agreement.
A caste of elderly initiates invokes the spirits of the water, acts as intermediary with the Creator and seeks solutions to the community's problems.
Respect for elders, of wives towards their husbands, of children towards everyone.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; men mostly take wives from outside, since one avoids marrying a woman from one's grandmother's group of origin.
The boy becomes a man through circumcision and rites in sacred places; the girl, when she has mastered running a household and good manners.
Steps: marriage proposal, acceptance, family meal.
Palm wine and cola seal the union; red oil, whisky and above all the mimpangá ledi, small shells, show the value of the woman.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Cult of the jengu, water spirit (the mermaid), celebrated every January by initiates and heads of family on the bank of the Sanaga.
The places of worship, on the riverbank or near the graves, evoke the former villages and the spirits of the ancestors.
Birth is a joy that enlarges the group; death, a divine punishment or a transfiguration. The deceased are called upon to obtain help or intercession.
Taboos: incest, adultery, murder, striking a parent.
Men and women practise divination with the lemon or the shells of mimpangá ledi.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: fishing, hunting, farming. Women: farming, home, small-scale fishing.
The land belongs to the community; it is accessed by putting it to productive use.
Ancestral crafts: dugout canoes, spears, drums and tam-tams.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Men: wrapper, shirt, chechia, sandals (formerly loincloth); women: kaba, headscarf, sandals.
Traditional medicine is appreciated because it is inexpensive.
Beauty: the strong, robust man with a broad chest; the woman with well-styled, beautiful hair, full-figured.
Courtship: good dancer, hard worker, hunter or fisherman; the woman a good dancer, well coiffed, with good manners.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: assiko, sèkèlè, mbayè; instruments: tam-tam, drum, piece of iron, bottle, whistle, Chinese bamboo.
Popular dances for rejoicing; sacred dances for mourning, enthronements and healing.
Festival: the ihangabinde, once a year, to call for divine help and make the land fertile.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: By their history and customs, the Malimba resemble the other Sawa peoples: Basaa, Banen, Duala, Bakoko.

sections.title: The names
items: Only twins have a particular mark: they are called diaha.
The name recalls the event that marked the birth and does not change.
People are often called by a pseudonym; women did not utter the name of a third person.
The founder, Elimbe (Elembe), is the son of Bendi, ancestor of the great Sawa group.

lessons.title: Who are the Malimba? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Malimba community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Malimba community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Malimba community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Malimba community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Malimba community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Malimba call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Minority group, alongside the more numerous Babimbi, and the Duala, Bakoko and Banen; the Malimba also speak Basaa and Bakoko. • Malimba is also spoken at Mouanko and Manoka (Douala). • Homogeneous group: marriages take place mostly within the group and with neighbours. • Ancestral land, to which one is linked as by the umbilical cord: every Malimba must feel at home there. • Coming from the Congo behind the founder Bendi, they lived on the Dibamba, at Dizangué, at Mouanko and by the ocean; all know themselves to be descended from one ancestor.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: A small Sawa fishing people, the Malimba say they descend from Elimbe, son of Bendi, the ancestor who came from Congo. Settled along the Sanaga and the ocean, between Dizangué and Logasse, alongside the Duala, Bakoko, Banen and Babimbi, they honour the water spirits through the jengu and celebrate the ihangabinde every year.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Malimba community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Malimba
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Malimba organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Malimba village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Malimba organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Malimba village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • Four groups each had their own chief under the Germans; under the French administration, they united under a single chief. • Decisions are made at the chiefdom, or at the canton between villages, by consensus among notables, heads of family, and village and canton chiefs. • The widow is free; in the past, unmarried people only saw each other after the parents' agreement. • A caste of elderly initiates invokes the water spirits, acts as an intermediary with the Creator and seeks solutions to the community's problems. • Respect for elders, of wives towards their husbands, of children towards everyone.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Four groups each had their own chief under the Germans; under the French administration, they united under a single chief. Decisions are made at the chiefdom, or at the canton between villages, by consensus among notables, heads of family, and village and canton chiefs. The widow is free; formerly, unmarried people only associated after the parents' agreement.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Malimba, then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Malimba
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Malimba, describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Malimba.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Malimba, describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Malimba.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: cassava and cassava sticks, fish in all its forms, game. • Drinks: palm wine. • Men: fishing, hunting, farming. Women: farming, home, small-scale fishing.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Malimba mainly eat cassava and cassava sticks, fish in all its forms, game. Traditional drinks: palm wine. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Malimba: write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Malimba
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth
lessons.competence: Explain how the Malimba welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Malimba family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Malimba welcome a child, give it a name and mark its entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A child has just been born in a Malimba family. How will they be named, and how will they become an adult?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Only twins have a special mark: they are called diaha. • The name recalls the event that marked the birth and does not change. • People are often called by a pseudonym; women did not pronounce the name of a third person. • Birth is a joy that enlarges the group; death, a divine punishment or a transfiguration. The dead are called upon for help or intercession. • A boy becomes a man through circumcision and rites in sacred places; a girl, when she has mastered running the household and good manners.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Only twins have a particular mark: they are called diaha. The name recalls the event that marked the birth and does not change. People often call each other by a pseudonym; women did not utter the name of a third person.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Malimba, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Malimba. First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: fishing, hunting, farming. Women: farming, home, small-scale fishing. • Land belongs to the community; access is by developing it. • Ancestral crafts: dugout canoes, spears, drums and tom-toms.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: fishing, hunting, farming. Women: farming, home, small-scale fishing. Land belongs to the community; it is accessed by developing it.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Malimba's activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

activities.title: I propose
activities.instruction: Suggest a project idea that promotes a local skill.

student.memo: Men: fishing, hunting, farming. Women: farming, home, small-scale fishing. Land belongs to the community; it is accessed by developing it.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Malimba
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Malimba, and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Malimba. Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Malimba, and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Malimba. Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Worship of the jengu, water spirit (the mermaid), celebrated every January by initiates and family heads on the banks of the Sanaga. • The places of worship, on the riverbank or near graves, evoke the old villages and the spirits of the ancestors. • Birth is a joy that enlarges the group; death, a divine punishment or a transfiguration. The dead are called upon for help or intercession. • Taboos: incest, adultery, murder, striking a parent. • Men and women practise divination with lemon or the shells of mimpangá ledi.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Cult of the jengu, water spirit (the mermaid), celebrated every January by initiates and heads of family on the bank of the Sanaga. The places of worship, on the riverbank or near the graves, evoke the former villages and the spirits of the ancestors.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Malimba (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Malimba
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Malimba and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Malimba family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Malimba greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Malimba family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Malimba. • Greetings: bunyababwam = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Dibabwam = morning greeting (one person); Edibabwam = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Ewo, Bebâ, Belalo, Benei, Betan. • The founder, Elimbe (Elembe), is the son of Bendi, ancestor of the great Sawa group. • In their history and customs, the Malimba resemble the other Sawa peoples: Basaa, Banen, Duala, Bakoko.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Malimba are the first steps towards communicating with the Malimba. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Malimba.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Malimba are the first steps towards communicating with the Malimba. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
